messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: beta
parts:
For starters, there is a bit of potential confusion in beta_log() in

src/maths/special_functions.hpp

refers to the log of the beta(a,b) *function*, whereas beta_log() in

src/stan/prob/distributions/beta_distribution.hpp

refers to the log of the beta(y, alpha, beta) *density*. So even
though they have different signatures, maybe we should change one of
the names?

Also, the textbook version of the beta distribution is usually defined
in terms of two shape parameters, which is how Bob and / or Daniel did
it for stan. However, when modeling a proportion with covariates and
an inverse link function, it is customary to parameterize the beta
distribution in terms of the mean (mu) and a precision parameter
(phi), where

mu := alpha / (alpha + beta)
phi := alpha + beta

See section 2 of http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/betareg/vignettes/betareg.pdf
for details.

I have added wrappers for these mu / phi parameterizations with names
beta_ls_log() and beta_binomial_ls_log() (with "ls" for location-
scale). The question I have is how is the user supposed to access them
in the .stan file that simply references "the" beta density? Of
course, users could implement the mu / phi parameterizations
themselves with local shape parameters in the model block:

double alpha
double beta

for(i in 1:I) {
mu <- inv_logit(something);
alpha <- mu * phi
beta <- (1.0 - mu) * phi;
y[i] ~ beta(y[i], alpha, beta);
}

But how can we save the user the trouble of converting from mu / phi
to alpha / beta? Does it need to say something like

y[i] ~ beta_ls(y[i], mu, phi)

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] beta

Just a warning. If we keep adding new features, we
have to test them, and it pushes the release back.

Answers to the substantive questions inline.

On 1/18/12 1:46 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> For starters, there is a bit of potential confusion in beta_log() in
>
> src/maths/special_functions.hpp
>
> refers to the log of the beta(a,b) *function*, whereas beta_log() in
>
> src/stan/prob/distributions/beta_distribution.hpp
>
> refers to the log of the beta(y, alpha, beta) *density*. So even
> though they have different signatures, maybe we should change one of
> the names?

We can't really easily change the name of the distribution.
So how about calling the beta function as:

beta_fun(a,b)

> Also, the textbook version of the beta distribution is usually defined
> in terms of two shape parameters, which is how Bob and / or Daniel did
> it for stan. However, when modeling a proportion with covariates and
> an inverse link function, it is customary to parameterize the beta
> distribution in terms of the mean (mu) and a precision parameter
> (phi), where
>
> mu := alpha / (alpha + beta)
> phi := alpha + beta

I like that parameterization. It's in the first hierarchical
model example in BDA.

> See section 2 of http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/betareg/vignettes/betareg.pdf
> for details.
>
> I have added wrappers for these mu / phi parameterizations with names
> beta_ls_log() and beta_binomial_ls_log() (with "ls" for location-
> scale).

Perfect.

Did you add corresponding unit tests in both the
double and agrad form?

> The question I have is how is the user supposed to access them
> in the .stan file that simply references "the" beta density? Of
> course, users could implement the mu / phi parameterizations
> themselves with local shape parameters in the model block:
>
> double alpha
> double beta
>
> for(i in 1:I) {
> mu<- inv_logit(something);
> alpha<- mu * phi
> beta<- (1.0 - mu) * phi;
> y[i] ~ beta(y[i], alpha, beta);
> }
That will work. It's what I've done in BUGS.

> But how can we save the user the trouble of converting from mu / phi
> to alpha / beta? Does it need to say something like
>
> y[i] ~ beta_ls(y[i], mu, phi)

Yes, that'll be the way it'll work as long as you
added beta_ls to the stan::prob namespace and it's
in the include (which I'm messing with now).

We've had lots of reparameterizations on the to-do
list for a while. Along with more cumulative densities.

It's so far been all we can do to get everything running
as is.

> Ben
>
